You are a visionary competing to satisfy the energy demand of a developing, solar-punk world. Fulfill the most demand using the cleanest forms of energy to score the most points and win! Your industry is built by playing cards on five revolving sectors over 12 rounds. Each sector you activate changes the power and configuration of all of your cards, creating a perpetually rearranging engine that will have you feeling like a true innovator! Manage your cards correctly to perform chains of actions across sectors and pull off supercharged combos. You’ll never use the same strategy twice! Shuffle in your choice of the available Tech Packs to instantly add exciting new technologies and tactics to discover. Test your skills in various challenging Solo mode scenarios, or play competitively and earn your place at the forefront of the energy revolution! Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Fundamental Concepts 2.1 Industry Sectors 2.2 Research 2.3 Breakthroughs 3 Round Structure 4 Game End and Scoring 4.1 Tech Pack Icons 5 Solo Mode Overview Welcome, innovator, to Electrify! It is up to you to provide electricity to a blossoming solar-punk world. In each of 12 rounds you will choose 1 of 5 sectors of your industry to activate. Each industry card you buy and place on sectors will add to the icons available when that sector is used and improve your engine. At the end of the 12th round, the player with the most energy points ​ from fulfilling demand goals and performing research wins. Most of the game is simultaneous. BGA will progress to the next round when all players have ended their previous round and selected their sector for the next round. Otherwise, all actions can be taken simultaneously. Your actions will be hidden from other players until all players have ended their turns and locked in their actions. Fundamental Concepts Your Player Board represents your energy network. The seven columns represent different energy sources, from the dirtiest (fossil fuel) on the left to the cleanest (solar) on the right. Energy cubes on the bottom partition of your board represent energy in your DEPOTS. They can be spent for cards, developed into better cubes, and transmitted to the grid. Energy cubes transmitted to the top partition of your board have been sent out to the GRID. They can be spent to fulfill demand goals or to perform research, but may no longer be spent to buy Industry Cards. Production (green) industry cards will allow you to generate more energy cubes, and can be discarded at any time for fossil fuel. Infrastructure (blue) industry cards allow you to do most everything else. When you draw cards, you choose how many you wish to draw from each deck. You may never have more than 9 cards in your hand. If an effect would cause you to draw above 9 cards, the additional cards are lost. Industry Sectors Your five Industry Sectors are arranged below your Player Board. Their position is important: the further to the right a sector is, the more powerful its actions become, based on the Clean ( ​ ) and Dirty ( ​ ) tracks above the sectors. Look for the matching green and black badges on icons, as they will multiply that icon by the value of the corresponding track in its column when used. Some icons also have a static multiplier (E.g. ​ ) that never changes. When a sector is charged, you gain access to the actions on the sector and on any cards you have played on it. Some cards also have arrows ( ​ ) that charge other cards, creating chains of available actions across your industry. At the end of each round, the sector you selected is reset to the first column. [Rating: 1/10] There really wasn't anything compelling about this game for me. Create cubes, move cubes, spend cubes. While you are generating an engine, it certainly isn't exciting or appealing. And the rounds go so fast that it doesn't feel like you are doing much. I won't ever buy this game.

[Rating: 4/10] planning the most efficient turn possible, considering action activation order and tons of resource convertion is not my cup of tea. And this game is all about that. By the end game you are doing a kajillion actions and moving a billion cubes.

[Rating: 4/10] Theme's cool and it can get really combotastic which can be fun or not. Barely any player interaction is not so much fun. I really dislike having player aid clarifying some of the iconography, but not all of it. Then sitting with cards in my hand not knowing what they do and losing the whole idea of interactions within my player board and what I could be doing.

[Rating: 5/10] I generally enjoy John D. Clair designs but I found this one a bit more hum drum than many of his games. I appreciated being able to add cards to improve the different tiles but the process of moving cubes to transmission side and only grabbing the second benefit on your first two contracts tedious and/or odd.  I also would need to check out the research? track where you can get other benefits and points out a bit further.  The game is also quite low scoring so you need to grab all the points you can wherever you can.

[Rating: 5/10] Always happy when publishers put games on BGA, and Electrify looked like an interesting engine builder. Unfortunately, after a few plays, I’m finding it pretty underwhelming.  The core loop is pick an action tile, Ark Nova-style, then move some cubes around. You have seven different types of energy, and most of your turn is spent adding, moving, and converting those cubes on your player board. Cubes on the bottom can be spent to add cards to your action tiles and make them more powerful, while cubes transmitted to the top help fulfill demands for points. Rinse and repeat for 12 rounds. [Rating: 5/10] Barely a game. A bit of a puzzle with some interesting stuff in there, but since it's nearly zero interaction I'm not going back to it.

[Rating: 6/10] 1 play on BGA.  Its got some fun stuff, but at least in my one game, it was all a lead up to then complete multiple goals at once in round 11 of 12.   And then 12 was for nothing.  I think its fine.

[Rating: 6.5/10] I played it twice on bga and it was ok. The thing that bothers me the most is that it's hard to plan for any given action bump so it never feel great even when it happens.   Also, since you can customize any given action, it gets to a point where these actions lose their identity, like it doesn't matter if this one was called "research" because it might very well become your best production action if you make it so.  I wish that the game would be more restrictive in certain area. For instance, having cards that could only be place in 1-2 actions could have great.
